messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun was twenty-nine, a painter by trade, married for three years to a woman he had met through family. The mugging happened on a Tuesday evening in late autumn, after he had finished a job in a neighborhood he knew his wife would have told him to avoid. A man came out from between two parked cars, knife already drawn, and demanded his wallet. Arjun remembered the blade catching the streetlight, the man’s hoarse voice repeating *give it*, and the terrible stillness of his own body as he complied. What he could not remember, no matter how hard he tried, was how he had gotten from that moment to the corner store where he finally called his wife. The minutes between were gone, a hole in the sequence. And that hole—the feeling that he must have frozen, must have done something wrong—filled with guilt each time he tried to piece it together deliberately.

The nightmares started almost immediately. He would wake at three in the morning, heart hammering, the dream already dissolving but the terror still thick in his chest, and lie there unable to move while the residue of the fear bled into the dark of the bedroom. His wife learned to sleep on the far edge of the mattress. By day, the fear attached itself to places. The alley where it happened became a place he would drive three blocks out of his way to avoid, but soon any alley, any narrow street between parked cars, any patch of shadow near a doorway, made his shoulders lock. When he drove to a new job site—and his work took him into dozens of unfamiliar neighborhoods every month—he would spend the first ten minutes scanning every face, every doorway, every hand that dropped to a pocket. His body stayed tense from the moment he parked until the moment he left; he could feel the readiness in his jaw, his fists, the back of his neck. He had always been an even-tempered man, but now a client’s offhand comment about the paint color could send him into an angry outburst that left him shaking and ashamed afterward. He snapped at his wife for leaving the front door unlocked. He stopped answering his phone.

He had come to believe that people could not be trusted. It was not a general suspicion—it was a certainty, rooted in that one encounter but spreading outward to cover every stranger, every neighbor, every friend who did not call back quickly enough. He felt isolated, set apart from people who had not been through what he had, and he was convinced that no one—not his wife, not his brothers—could actually help him if something went wrong. He had to watch for danger himself, and that meant he could never relax. When his wife tried to comfort him after a nightmare, he pulled away. What could she possibly understand? The mistrust made him see threats where there were none: a man walking too briskly on the sidewalk became a potential attacker, and the sight of that man (a trigger that the mistrust itself had created) would send Arjun’s body on alert and, sometimes, bring back a fragment of the memory—the glint of the knife, the voice—that made his chest tighten and his guilt surge. The guilt, in turn, reinforced his belief that he was alone in this, that he could not rely on others, because if he had been stronger he would have fought back, and then he would not need anyone.

The cycle tightened over months. A spatial trigger—a particular street corner, a bus stop with a similar streetlight—would set off the scanning and the flash of memory, and that memory (incomplete as it was) would spike his tension and deepen his sense of isolation. His constant vigilance meant he noticed more ambiguous cues, which became new triggers, and each new trigger made him jump or snap. At work, he started turning down jobs in neighborhoods that matched the one where he had been robbed, even when it cost him money. His wife gave him an ultimatum after he yelled at her for touching his shoulder from behind. He came to the clinic because he was afraid he was losing his marriage, and because he was exhausted from the constant, low-grade terror that had not let up in over a year. What he wanted, he said, was to feel like himself again—but what he feared most, when he let himself think about it, was that the man with the knife had taken that possibility away for good.
